title: Bursitis: reducing irritation and recognising possible infection
intro: Bursae are small fluid-containing sacs that reduce friction between tissues near joints. When a bursa becomes inflamed, the area may be painful, tender or swollen. Bursitis can affect places such as the shoulder, hip, elbow or knee. Repeated pressure, injury and some other illnesses can contribute, but an infected bursa needs different care. Not every painful joint or visible swelling is bursitis.

sections.heading: Describe the location and what provokes symptoms
paragraphs: Tell the clinician where it hurts, when swelling began and which movements or pressure make it worse. Kneeling, leaning on elbows or a change in repetitive activity may be relevant. Mention a fall, scrape, puncture, recent procedure, gout or inflammatory arthritis. Some bursae are close to the skin and visibly swell; deeper problems may mainly cause pain. Similar symptoms can come from tendons, arthritis or joint infection, so do not diagnose the cause only from a photograph or the fact that activity provokes it.

sections.heading: Seek earlier assessment for a hot or rapidly worsening area
paragraphs: Increasing heat, spreading redness, marked tenderness, fever, chills or feeling unwell needs prompt medical assessment, particularly after a skin break or with diabetes or reduced immunity. Redness may be harder to see on darker skin, so warmth, swelling and general illness matter too. Severe pain or inability to move or use the joint needs urgent advice. Confusion, collapse or serious breathing difficulty requires emergency help. Do not put a needle into the swelling, squeeze it or assume a familiar bursitis diagnosis rules out a new infection.

sections.heading: Understand examination and selective testing
paragraphs: The clinician examines the area, joint movement and surrounding skin and asks about your health. Tests depend on the findings; not every case needs a scan. Sometimes fluid is sampled to look for infection or crystals, or imaging helps investigate a different cause. Ask what a proposed test would change and whether infection has been considered before any injection. Bring a medicine list, including anticoagulants and treatments that affect immunity. A recurring swelling or poor response deserves reassessment instead of repeatedly accepting an uncertain label.

sections.heading: Reduce pressure while keeping recovery practical
paragraphs: When infection and serious injury have been excluded, temporarily modify the activity or direct pressure that aggravates the bursa. Padding, a different working position or breaks may help. A cold pack wrapped in cloth can ease symptoms; protect the skin and stop if it becomes painfully cold or numb. Ask about suitable pain medicines with your health and other treatments. Balance rest with movement recommended for the affected area rather than immobilising it indefinitely. A physiotherapist can help adjust loading and technique when needed.

sections.heading: Review treatment options and recurrence
paragraphs: Infected bursitis may need antibiotics and sometimes drainage under medical supervision. For selected non-infected problems, an injection may be discussed after weighing benefit and risks; it is not suitable for every painful swelling. Surgery is uncommon and depends on persistent symptoms or complications. Agree a review plan, how to return to work or sport and what changes require earlier contact. Recurrence can mean the original pressure is continuing or another condition needs treatment. Improvement should be judged by pain and function, not a promise that a swelling will disappear by a fixed date.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: changing pressure at work
examples.text: A worker develops swelling over the kneecap after repeated kneeling. After assessment excludes infection and significant injury, they discuss padding, task changes and a gradual return. They do not repeatedly drain the swelling themselves to get through each shift.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: new warmth and fever
examples.text: Someone with previous elbow bursitis develops rapidly increasing pain, warmth and fever after a small scrape. They seek prompt assessment and report the broken skin rather than treating it as the same uncomplicated flare and requesting another steroid injection.

questions: Is this bursitis, and are infection, crystals or another joint problem possible?
Which activity changes, pain relief or investigations are appropriate for this location and my health?
Would further treatment help, and what should prompt review sooner or urgent care?
